CLINICAL BACKGROUND

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is mainly a disease of childhood that arises from recurrent genetic alterations that block precursor B- and T-cell differentiation and drive aberrant cell proliferation and survival. The genetic alterations can now be identified in more than 80% of cases of ALL. These genetic lesions influence the prognosis and therapeutic approach used for treatment of ALLs.

The commonly detected chromosomal translocations and fusion genes in B-lineage ALL (B-ALL) are:

  • E2A-PBX1; t(1;19)(q23;p13) - This translocation is the one of the most frequent translocations in B- ALL and is observed in both adult and pediatric population at an overall frequency of 6%. This is associated with good prognosis.
  • TEL-AML1; t(12;21)(p13;q22) - This translocation is the most common alteration in pediatric cancer and occurs in approximately 25% of B-ALL cases. This is associated with good prognosis.
  • MLL rearrangement-These are frequent genetic aberrations resulting in high risk ALL, and are associated with poor prognosis.
  • BCR-ABL1;t(9;22)(q34;q11) - BCR/ABL-positive ALL is the most common genetic abnormality associated with adult ALL and has been shown to confer the worst prognosis to both children and adults. The t(9;22) occurs in 25–30% of adult and 3–5% of childhood B-cell ALL.
